Here is a concise, print-ready 12-week postpartum program summary tailored for a 33-year-old client, four weeks post uncomplicated C-section, with mat-only equipment (yoga mat). It combines Foundation/Phase 1 (weeks 1–4), Phase 2 (weeks 5–6), and Phase 3 (weeks 7–12) with integrated strength, cardio, core progression, and the cardio/HIIT notes you requested (HIIT delayed until Phase 3 and only with clearance). It emphasizes pelvic floor health, diastasis monitoring, gradual loading, and a 4-day-per-week structure (2 mobility/recovery days, 2 main strength days) with an optional light cardio day. All movements avoid heavy abdominal loading until cleared and focus on diaphragmatic breathing, core coordination, and safe progression.

Phase 1: Weeks 1–4 — Foundation, pelvic floor, and gentle conditioning
Goals
- Re-establish diaphragmatic breathing and pelvic floor control.
- Introduce safe hip/knee-friendly movements; restore hip hinge and glute engagement.
- Begin safe upper-body patterns; protect the core and avoid abdominal loading.

Weekly structure
- 4 days/week: 2 mobility/recovery days, 2 main strength days; optional 5th day light cardio.

Key components per week
- Week 1
  - Session A (Mobility + Pelvic Floor): diaphragmatic breathing, 3 rounds x6 breaths; 3x8–10 Kegels; 2x10 pelvic tilts; 2x8 Cat-Cow; 2x8–10 glute bridges; cool-down 2 minutes Child’s Pose.
  - Session B (Lower Body Mobility + Core Prep): 2–3 sets 30s hip flexor and hamstring sweeps; 3x8–10 glute bridges; 2x10 side-lying clams; 2–3x8 dead bug progressions; 2x30s marching in place; 2 minutes diaphragmatic breathing.
  - Daily: 10-minute walk; 5 minutes pelvic floor contractions after walks.
- Week 2
  - Session A (Breath + Pelvic Floor): 5 rounds of 6 breaths; 4x10 Kegels; 3x12 bridges; 2–3 sets 6 dead bugs; 2x8 bird-dogs (partial); 2x8 standing hip hinge; cool-down 3 minutes.
  - Session B (Upper Body Safe Patterns): seated rows or towel rows 2–3x8–10; wall/ incline push-ups 2–3x8–12; 2 rounds 30s shoulder mobility; dead bug or dead bug with partial knee extension 2–3x6–8; pelvic floor breath 2 minutes.
  - Optional: 15–20 minute walk.
- Week 3
  - Session A (Mobility + Core Activation): 4–5 rounds diaphragmatic breathing; 5x8–12 pelvic floor activation; side-lying leg lifts 2–3x8; supine bridges with gentle march 2–3x8–10; modified dead bug 3x8 per side.
  - Session B (Lower/Upper Body Stability): seated rows 3x10; incline push-ups 3x8–10; scapular push-ups on wall 2–3x12; Pallof-esque bracing 2–3x8–10s; core dead bugs 2–3x6–8.
  - Mobility after meals: 10–15 minutes.
- Week 4
  - Session A (Light Loading Intro): diaphragmatic breathing with pelvic floor 5–6 rounds; hip hinge 2–3x8 with light tempo; bridges with march 3x10; side-lying leg extension 2–3x10; bird-dog progression 1–2 per side.
  - Session B (Upper Body Strength Intro): seated rows or light resistance 3x10–12; incline or wall push-ups 3x8–12; shoulder mobility 2 rounds; dead bug 3x8; light cardio 10–15 minutes.
Notes
- Six-week OB clearance is assumed for any deeper loading after week 6.
- If bleeding/pain/diastasis worsens, revert to Week 3 patterns and consult clinician.

Phase 2: Weeks 5–6 — Introduce light resistance and structured loading
Goals
- Add light resistance and defined loading while preserving pelvic floor integrity.
- Begin lower-body pushing/pulling and maintain core safety.

Weekly structure
- 4 days/week; 3 strength days + optional cardio.

Week 5
- Session A (Pelvic Floor + Basic Strength): 5 rounds diaphragmatic breathing with pelvic floor; hip hinges 3x10 with light dumbbell/kettlebell or bodyweight; glute bridge with single-leg progression 2–3x8 per side; standing marching with light load 2–3x20s; dead bug with alternate limb extension 3x6 per side.
- Session B (Lower Body Strength): goblet squats 3x8–10 (light); step-ups 3x8 per leg; glute bridges 3x12; light rows 2–3x12; incline push-ups 3x8–12; core dead bugs 3x8.
- Optional cardio: 12–20 minute easy walk.
- Core progression: continue with diaphragmatic breathing while bracing; avoid any traditional sit-ups.

Week 6
- Session A (Full-Body Light Load): hip hinge + light deadlift pattern 3x8; split squats 2–3x8 per leg; glute bridges 3x12; Pallof hold 2–3x8–10s; side planks with knee down 2–3x15–20s if cleared.
- Session B (Upper Body Strength): dumbbell rows or resistance band rows 3x10–12; incline or floor press 3x8–12; shoulder external rotations 2–3x12; anti-rotation carry or Pallof hold 2–3x8–10s per side; mobility work.
- Cardio: 20–30 minutes 3–4 days/week; 1–2 intervals of brisk walking added if tolerated.

Phase 3: Weeks 7–12 — Build strength, add push/pull intensity, and integrate cardio progression
Goals
- Strength focus with safe progression; push intensity increased in weeks 7–12 per plan.
- Maintain pelvic floor and diastasis safety while increasing load and volume.
- Cardiovascular conditioning continues with progressive duration and intervals.

Weekly structure
- 4 days/week formal plan (2 strength days, 2 mobility/recovery days); optional 5th light cardio day.
- Cardio progression aligned with weeks (see cardio plan below).
- HIIT adds only after Phase 3 readiness criteria are met and clinician clearance is obtained (weeks 7–12, with strict safeguards; see HIIT notes).

Phase 3 Strength: Weeks 7–12 push focus
Week 7
- Push/pull emphasis:
  - Incline dumbbell press or floor press: 3–4x8–10; tempo 2–0-2
  - Push-ups (incline or floor): 3x6–10
  - Dumbbell shoulder press (neutral grip) or standing overhead press: 2–3x8–10
- Core/pelvic: anti-rotation and bracing; dead bugs or Pallof holds
- Tempo and rest: 2–0-2; 60–90s rest

Week 8
- Heavier load cues:
  - Floor press or incline press: 3–4x8–10 with slightly heavier weight
  - Push-ups progression: 3x8–12; paused reps at chest if possible
  - Overhead press: 2–3x6–8 or 8–10 with light-moderate load
  - Row variation (pull): 3x10–12
- Core: Pallof holds 2–3x12–15s; side planks knee-down if cleared
- Conditioning: keep to 30–40 minutes cardio as per plan

Week 9
- Push density and volume:
  - Horizontal press: 4x6–8 with moderate weight
  - Incline push-ups: 3–4x6–10
  - Floor press or light push press: 2–3x6–8
  - Shoulder work: external rotations 2–3x8–10
- Core stability: anti-rotation carries 2–3x20–30s per side
- Frequency: two push sessions that week if energy allows

Week 10
- Strength with controlled volume:
  - Chest press pattern: 3–4x6–8
  - Push-ups or tempo push-ups: 3–4x8–10
  - Rows or pull variations: 3x10–12
  - Shoulder health: 2–3x8–10 external rotations
- Tempo and load: slower eccentrics (2–3s)
- Core: Pallof holds 15s, anti-rotation carries 20–30s

Week 11
- Peak pushing block:
  - Push variations: 4x6 reps at challenging but doable load
  - Ladder incline to floor press: 3x8–10
  - Overhead press: 2–3x6–8
  - Accessory: supported dips if cleared; otherwise floor press
- Core: anti-rotation carries, side planks as tolerated

Week 12
- Target week to feel strong:
  - Push-pull: main push movement 3–4x6–8 (e.g., floor press or incline press)
  - Secondary push: push-ups or dumbbell shoulder press 3–4x8–10
  - Pulling: row variations or face pulls 3x10–12
  - Optional conditioning finisher: short circuit (3 rounds, 40s work/20s rest)
- Core/pelvic: maintain bracing; light core sets if cleared

Cardio progression (weeks 1–12)
- Weeks 1–4: 15–20 minutes, walking; optional 5-minute post-workout walk
- Weeks 5–6: 20–30 minutes with occasional 1-minute brisk intervals
- Weeks 7–9: 30–35 minutes with 1–2 intervals of 2 minutes brisk
- Weeks 10–12: 35–45 minutes, 2–4 intervals of 1–2 minutes brisk; optional longer steady-state blocks
- HIIT: consider only after Week 12, Phase 3, with clinician clearance; begin with 4–6 minutes total work (8x20s at RPE 6–7 with 40–60s rest), low impact, and progress slowly (see HIIT guidelines below)

Optional HIIT—when to add (only if ready and cleared)
- Phase: Phase 3 (Weeks 7–12) and only after readiness:
  - Start with very low volume: 4–6 minutes total work per session
  - Structure: 8 rounds of 20s high-intensity (RPE 6–7/10) with 40–60s easy
  - Modality: low-impact walking intervals, stationary cycling with minimal resistance, or similar
  - Frequency: 1–2 HIIT sessions per week, separated by at least 48 hours
  - Cues: avoid Valsalva, maintain diaphragmatic breathing, pelvic floor engaged
  - Stop if: leakage, pain, or diastasis worsens; revert to steady-state cardio

Core reintroduction and progression (summary)
- Weeks 1–4: diaphragmatic breathing, pelvic floor activation, dead bugs, pelvic tilts, no loaded abs
- Weeks 5–6: introduce light, non-bracing abdominal cues; dead bugs with limb movement; Pallof holds if tolerated
- Weeks 7–12: progressive transverse abdominal bracing and anti-rotation work; carries; controlled bracing with breath; avoid loaded crunch-type movements
- Stop or revert if doming, leakage, pain, or diastasis widening occurs

Nutrition and recovery (brief recap)
- Calorie target: approx. 300–500 calories/day above non-pregnant maintenance; adjust by appetite, milk supply, and weight trends
- Protein: 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day; distribute 20–40 g protein per meal
- Hydration: 2.5–3.5 L/day (more with breastfeeding)
- Breastfeeding considerations: monitor output; hydration; caffeine limit ~200–300 mg/day; avoid alcohol per lactation guidelines
- Sleep and stress: prioritize rest; nap when possible; manage workload

Progression criteria and safety
- Progress only when: no new symptoms, diastasis stable/improved, pelvic floor function solid during core work, and clinician clearance for increases
- Red flags: bleeding, sharp abdominal pain, persistent back pain near scar, leakage, or worsening symptoms

Customization options
- If you’d like, I can tailor this summary to a precise weekly schedule with exact exercise names, reps, sets, and load progression based on her current strength level, equipment available, and any diastasis measurements. I can also generate a printable, week-by-week plan and a client-facing one-page summary.

Here's a structured 12-week postpartum return-to-exercise plan tailored for a 33-year-old, four weeks post uncomplicated C-section, cleared for light activity at four weeks with OB clearance for light activity and no abdominal or heavy lifting until six weeks. The plan uses only a yoga mat and emphasizes gradual reintroduction of movement, core restoration, pelvic floor engagement, and overall conditioning while respecting the healing process. Progressions are cautious and criteria-based; if any red flags arise (bleeding, increased pain, pelvic floor distress, diastasis symptoms, dizziness), pause and consult the client's medical provider.

Important notes at the start
- Core restrictions: No traditional planks, sit-ups, crunches, or deep resisted abdominal work until cleared at six weeks. Emphasize diaphragmatic breathing, pelvic floor engagement, and gentle abdominal bracing.
- Pelvic floor focus: Integrate daily pelvic floor activation (Kegels) and breath coordination. Avoid heavy coughing or straining.
- Diastasis check: If the client notices a cone/tissue bulge with loading or abdominal bracing, back off and reassess guidance from a clinician.
- Recovery cues: Prioritize sleep, hydration, and gentle mobility; workouts should feel manageable and not fatiguing.

Weekly structure
- Weekly frequency: 4 days/week of focused sessions (2 short mobility/recovery days, 2 main conditioning/strength days). Optional 5th day with light activity like walking or gentle yoga if energy allows.
- Session length: 20–35 minutes on conditioning days; 15–25 minutes on mobility days.
- Warm-up: 3–5 minutes of gentle movement (breathwork, diaphragmatic breathing, hip circles, ankle/shoulder mobility).
- Cool-down: 3–5 minutes of gentle stretching and abdominal/diaphragmatic breathing.

Phase 1: Weeks 1–4 (4 weeks post-partum, light activity emphasis)
Goal: Re-establish breathing, pelvic floor control, and gentle hip/knee-friendly movements; begin low-load upper body safe patterns; maintain daily walking.

Week 1
- Session A (Mobility + Pelvic Floor Activation, 20–25 min)
  - Breathing and posture: 3 rounds of diaphragmatic breath x6 each, with pelvic floor engagement on exhale.
  - Pelvic floor activation: 3 sets of 8–10 Kegels, short squeezes held 2–3 seconds, relax fully between reps.
  - Pelvic tilts: 2 sets of 10 slow pelvic tilts (gentle 1–2 cm lift with exhale).
  - Cat-Cow (modified): 2 sets of 8, focus on spinal neutrality and breath.
  - Hip bridge (glute activation): 2 sets of 8–10 with gentle glute squeeze; avoid pushing through the lower back; ensure core is engaged, but no full abdominal bracing.
  - Cool-down: child's pose with deep breathing, 2 minutes.

- Session B (Light Lower-Body Mobility + Core prep, 25–30 min)
  - Mobility: 2–3 sets of 30 seconds each: hip flexor stretch (standing or prone), hamstring sweep (gentle).
  - Glute bridges: 3 sets of 8–10 with controlled tempo; no posterior pelvic tilt beyond neutral.
  - Side-lying clams: 2 sets of 10 per side, no resistance.
  - Dead bug progression (modified): 2–3 sets of 8 reps per side, keeping lower back pressed to mat, one leg at a time (no spine rounding).
  - Gentle marching in place: 2–3 sets of 30 seconds.
  - Breath work: 2 minutes diaphragmatic breathing.

- Daily micro-movements: 10-minute walk daily; 5 minutes of pelvic floor contractions after each walk.

Week 2
- Session A (Breath + Pelvic Floor Reinforcement, 25–30 min)
  - Diaphragmatic breathing with pelvic floor coordination: 5 rounds of 6 breaths.
  - Pelvic floor activation: 4 sets of 10 Kegels with 2–3 second hold.
  - Pelvic tilts and bridges: 3 sets of 12 bridges (gentle tempo; stop if any mid-back arch occurs).
  - Modified bird-dog: 2–3 sets of 6 per side (slow, controlled; knee/hand only if comfortable).
  - Standing hip hinge to neutral: 2 sets of 8 reps (hip hinge with minimal knee bend; avoid deep squats).
  - Cool-down: 3 minutes gentle hip/quad stretch in supine.

- Session B (Upper Body Safe Patterns, 25–35 min)
  - Seated or supine torso-friendly rows: use light resistance if available; if not, perform scapular retraction without loading spine. 2–3 sets of 8–10.
  - Wall push-ups progression: standing with hands on wall, 2–3 sets of 8–12; progress to countertop or incline push-ups as tolerable.
  - Shoulder mobility: 2 rounds of 30 seconds each (arm circles, wall slides if feasible).
  - Core prep: dead bug or dead bug with partial knee extension (as tolerable) 2–3 sets of 6–8.
  - Pelvic floor check-in: 2 minutes of breath with pelvic floor engagement after session.

- Optional: continue daily 15–20 minute walk; add gentle stroller walks if comfortable.

Week 3
- Session A (Mobility + Core Activation, 25–30 min)
  - Diaphragmatic breathing with 4–5 rounds.
  - Pelvic floor activation: 5 sets of 8–12 reps, add a 2-second hold.
  - Side-lying leg lifts: 2–3 sets of 8 per side (no hip hiking).
  - Supine bridges with a gentle march: 2–3 sets of 8–10; avoid arching.
  - Modified dead bug: 3 sets of 8 per side with slow tempo.
  - Hip mobility sequence: 2 rounds of seated/lying figure-4 stretch, 30–45 seconds per side.

- Session B (Low-Load Upper Body + Stability, 30–35 min)
  - Seated rows with light resistance or towel: 3 sets of 10.
  - Incline push-ups (on countertop/edge): 3 sets of 8–10.
  - Scapular push-ups on wall: 2–3 sets of 12.
  - Pallof-esque bracing: standing isometrics with a light resistance band if available; 2–3 sets of 8–10 seconds hold (avoid twisting).
  - Core awareness: 2–3 sets of 6 dead bugs, progressively extending limbs only if breath control remains.

- Movement snack: 10–15 minutes of mindful mobility after meals to aid digestion.

Week 4
Goal: Confirm readiness for six-week check and begin gentle, more controlled loading if symptoms allow. Maintain gentle pace.

- Session A (Reintroduction to Mild Loading, 30–35 min)
  - Diaphragmatic breathing with pelvic floor coordination (5–6 rounds).
  - Hip hinge patterns: 2–3 sets of 8 with light tempo, no squats yet.
  - Bridges with march: 3 sets of 10; keep core braced lightly and focus on neutral spine.
  - Side-lying leg extension: 2–3 sets of 10 per side.
  - Core prep: bird-dog progression to 1–2 per side with controlled tempo; avoid linking to heavy loads.

- Session B (Upper Body Strength Intro, 30–40 min)
  - Seated rows or band rows: 3 sets of 10–12.
  - Push-ups: incline or wall progression, 3 sets of 8–12.
  - Shoulder mobility and stability: 2 rounds of 30–40 seconds each.
  - Core-friendly: dead bug or dead bug with leg extension 3 sets of 8.
  - Light cardio: 10–15 minute easy walk.

Post-Week 4 note: Many clients may still be in early postpartum recovery. If any bleeding, pain, or separation (diastasis) worsens, revert to Week 3 patterns and consult clinician. At six weeks, with medical clearance, you can begin more formal progression.

Phase 2: Weeks 5–6 (Six-week check, potential clearance for light resistance)
Goal: Introduce light resistance, increase movement complexity slightly while preserving core and pelvic floor integrity.

Week 5
- Session A (Pelvic Floor + Basic Strength, 35–40 min)
  - Activation and breath: 5 rounds of diaphragmatic breathing with pelvic floor engagement.
  - Hip hinges: 3 sets of 10 with a light kettlebell or dumbbell if available or no load if not.
  - Glute bridge with single-leg progression: 2–3 sets of 8 per side.
  - Standing marching with light load: 2–3 sets of 20 seconds.
  - Core pattern: dead bug with alternate arm/leg extension 3 sets of 6 per side.

- Session B (Lower-Body Strength, 30–40 min)
  - Goblet squat to upright stand (no depth beyond pain-free): 3 sets of 8–10; use light weight if tolerated.
  - Step-ups or step-downs to a stable surface: 3 sets of 8 per leg.
  - Glute bridges with tempo: 3 sets of 12.
  - Latissimus/Scapular work: 2–3 sets of 12 rows with light resistance or towel.
  - Optional gentle cardio: 12–20 minute walk or light jog if cleared by clinician.

Week 6
- Session A (Full-Body Light Load, 40–45 min)
  - Warm-up with mobility.
  - Hip hinge + light deadlift pattern: 3 sets of 8 with light load (dumbbell).
  - Split squats: 2–3 sets of 8 per leg (bodyweight or light load).
  - Glute bridge variations: single-leg 2–3 sets of 8 per leg.
  - Core: modified side planks with knee down if cleared; otherwise, continue with dead bug progressions.
  - Cool-down: 5 minutes of gentle stretching.

- Session B (Upper Body Strength + Stability, 30–40 min)
  - Dumbbell rows or resistance band rows: 3 sets of 10–12.
  - Push-ups: incline progression 3 sets of 8–12.
  - Shoulder external rotation with bands or light dumbbells: 2–3 sets of 12.
  - Core: anti-rotation carry or Pallof hold (single-arm, light load) 2–3 sets of 8–10 seconds.
  - Mobility: hips, thoracic spine, and neck relaxation.

Phase 3: Weeks 7–12 (Return-to-Training Building Phase)
Goal: Build progressive strength and endurance, increase volume gradually, and reintroduce more functional movements while maintaining pelvic floor integrity.

Week 7
- Session A (Full-Body Strength, 40–45 min)
  - Warm-up: 5 minutes dynamic mobility.
  - Squats to a chair or box: 3 sets of 10–12.
  - Romanian deadlift with light dumbbells: 3 sets of 8–10.
  - Step-ups: 3 sets of 8–10 per leg.
  - Glute bridges with march: 3 sets of 12.
  - Core: dead bug to heel slide progression: 3 sets of 8 per side.

- Session B (Push/Pull + Stability, 35–45 min)
  - Push-ups (full or incline) or floor press with light dumbbells: 3 sets of 8–12.
  - Rows (opt: off a bench) 3 sets of 10–12.
  - Scapular stability: 3 rounds of 12 shoulder blade squeezes.
  - Pallof hold: 3 sets of 10 seconds per side.
  - Mobility: hip flexor and thoracic spine.

Week 8

- Sun exposure and vitamin D: Vitamin D status matters; consider a vitamin D supplement if not obtaining adequate sun exposure and per clinician guidance.
- Hydration: Carry a water bottle and sip frequently; include liquids with meals and snacks; hydration supports milk production.

- Use appetite and energy as primary guides for adjusting calories.
- Monitor weight and breastmilk volume (if feasible) and adjust intake accordingly.
- Revisit protein targets and ensure meals have 20–40 g protein per meal, especially around workouts.
- If fatigue or breast fullness becomes problematic, recalibrate volume, sleep strategies, and meal timing.

Great question. For a postpartum client, core reintroduction is a stepwise process that respects healing, diastasis, and pelvic floor function. Here’s a clear framework for when and how to reintroduce “abs” work safely.

Key principles
- Prioritize pelvic floor and core coordination first. Abs work should never override the pelvic floor or breath.
- Avoid traditional high-load abdominal exercises (crunches, sit-ups, V-ups) while healing or if diastasis is present or symptomatic.
- Introduce progressive abdominal loading only after: six weeks post-C-section with medical clearance, stable pelvic floor function, controlled bracing without doming or bulging, and ability to maintain diaphragmatic breathing during exertion.

Timing guidelines
- Weeks 0–6 (phase 1): Core work focuses on diaphragmatic breathing, pelvic floor activation, pelvic tilts, dead bugs with precise bracing, hetero- or anti-rotation basics, and diaphragmatic breathing with pelvic floor engagement. No loaded or dynamic abdominal curls. Core work limited to dead bugs, diaphragms, and gentle floor-based patterns as tolerable.
- Weeks 6–8 (phase 2, post-6-week clearance): If diastasis is stable or improved and there are no pelvic floor symptoms during core work, you can begin low-load, non-bracing abdominal cues. Begin with:
  - Modified dead bug progressions with leg/arm movement while maintaining neutral spine.
  - Pelvic tilts integrated with diaphragmatic breathing.
  - Gentle “braced” core activation without crunching (anterior bracing with breath, not pushing outward).
  - Avoid pulling the ribs toward the pelvis with excess force.
- Weeks 9–12 (phase 3): For clients with good pelvic floor function, no diastasis progression, and tolerance to bracing, introduce more targeted abdominal work:
  - Transverse abdominis-focused bracing drills (lid-like contraction) with breath, 4–6 sets of 6–10 seconds holds.
  - Stability-based movements that gently challenge the core, such as Pallof presses with light resistance, anti-rotation carries, and farmer walks (if equipment available). For mat-only, equivalents include resisted dead bug variations, pallof-inspired holds with a looped band or towel, side planks with knee down progressing to full side planks only if cleared.
  - Progress to regulated a few low-load exercises that recruit the abdominals indirectly, like plank regressions only if clinician clearance supports bracing with a neutral spine.

Practical exercise progression (examples)
- Week 6–7: 
  - Dead bug with light limb extension (3–4 sets of 6–8 per side) with controlled breath.
  - Diaphragmatic breathing with pelvic floor bracing during each rep.
  - Glute bridges with marching to maintain neutral spine and avoid abdominal doming.
- Week 8–9:
  - Bilateral dead bug variations with slight fingertip pressing on mat to cue neutral spine.
  - Pallof hold (anti-rotation) with light resistance for 8–12 seconds, 2–3 sets per side.
  - Side-lying clams but focus on keeping core engaged; progress to side planks with knee down if tolerance is solid.
- Week 10–12:
  - Transverse abdominis bracing holds (4–6 sets of 6–10 seconds) with controlled breathing.
  - Anti-rotation carries (light dumbbell or band) for 20–30 seconds, 2–3 sets per side.
  - Optional gentle floor-based “curl” progressions only if cleared by clinician and without diastasis widening.

Signs to stop or back off
- Any bulging or doming of the abdomen during abdominal bracing or loaded core work.
- Pelvic floor leakage, heaviness, or pain during or after core work.
- Severe lower back pain, abdominal pain near incision, or any bleeding.
- Worsening diastasis symptoms (gap widening with bracing).

How to communicate with the client
- Explain that “core” for postpartum clients is broader than the traditional abs. It’s about coordinated breathing, pelvic floor support, spinal bracing, and progressive load.
- Use clear cues: “breathe in with ribs wide, exhale and gently draw in the lower abdomen toward the spine without sucking in or flattening the back.”
- Track progression with simple criteria: can perform dead bugs and diaphragmatic breathing with good form for 3–4 weeks before calling for the next progression. If in doubt, consult her clinician.

Short answer: HIIT is not recommended early in the postpartum plan. With a C-section recovery and the need to re-establish pelvic floor function and core control, HIIT should be reserved until later phases and only after careful screening and clinician clearance.

Reasoning
- High-intensity intervals increase intra-abdominal pressure and spinal load, which can aggravate diastasis, pelvic floor symptoms, or scar tissue sensitivity.
- Postpartum tissue healing, sleep disruption, and breastfeeding considerations mean tolerance and recovery are variable; HIIT demands higher recovery capacity.
- The plan you’re using prioritizes diaphragmatic breathing, pelvic floor activation, and gradual loading. HIIT can undermine those if introduced too soon.

- Best to consider after Phase 3 (weeks 7–12) and only if:
  - Pelvic floor strength is robust without leakage or heaviness during daily activities and during core work.
  - Diastasis recti is stable or improved with no widening during bracing.
  - You have completed several weeks of progressive cardio and strength without adverse symptoms.
  - Medical clearance from the OB/physician confirms readiness for higher-intensity work.

How to introduce HIIT safely (only when eligible)
- Start with very low volume: 4–6 minutes of work time per session, total.
- Structure example:
  - 8 rounds of 20 seconds high-intensity work at a light to moderate intensity (RPE 6–7/10) followed by 40–60 seconds of easy pace or complete rest.
  - Choose low-impact modalities (fast walking intervals, stationary cycling at low resistance, or elliptical-like movements if available) to minimize spine and pelvic floor strain.
- Progression rules:
  - Only increase duration or intensity if no pelvic floor symptoms, no diastasis worsening, and you recover well between sessions.
  - Keep core bracing light and avoid Valsalva maneuvers; maintain diaphragmatic breathing throughout.
  - Never perform HIIT on days when you have fatigue, poor sleep, or any signs of lactation issues or dehydration.

- Preferably during Phase 3 (weeks 7–12) and only after you’ve established a solid cardio base and strength foundation.
- Limit to 1–2 HIIT sessions per week initially, with at least 48 hours between intense sessions to allow recovery.
- Always pair with a proper warm-up and cool-down, including pelvic floor activation and diaphragmatic breathing.

Monitoring and red flags
- Stop HIIT immediately if you notice any leakage, pelvic heaviness, or worsening diastasis during or after sessions.
- Watch for increased fatigue, sleep disruption, or signs of overtraining; back off and revert to moderate-intensity cardio until ready again.
